title: U.S. Marine Corps to Deploy Anti-Ship and Air-Defense Systems to Japan's Yonaguni for Exercise Keen Sword

content:
In a significant development for regional security, the U.S. Marine Corps is set to deploy advanced ground-based anti-ship and air-defense systems to Japan’s Yonaguni Island as part of the upcoming Keen Sword exercise. This deployment is particularly noteworthy due to Yonaguni’s strategic location, just 110 kilometers from Taiwan.

Keen Sword, the largest biennial joint military drill between the U.S. and Japan, will feature two critical systems from the Marine Corps’ littoral force: the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS). The local government of Yonaguni disclosed these deployment plans recently, coinciding with the Okinawa Defense Bureau’s announcement regarding the exercise.

This will mark the first time both NMESIS and MADIS are deployed on Yonaguni, reflecting a shift in focus toward multi-island, sea-denial operations. The U.S. and Japan are moving away from traditional heavy armored platforms and emphasizing mobile missile and air-defense systems capable of rapid deployment from scattered islands. NMESIS, in particular, can strike targets approximately 115 miles away, posing a potential threat to naval operations in the vicinity of Taiwan.

The announcement of this deployment has raised concerns among Chinese military analysts, especially as China’s PLA Navy and coast guard have been increasingly active near Taiwan. The NMESIS and MADIS systems are part of the Marine Corps’ modernization efforts to create small, agile forces capable of rapid island capture and defense.

Earlier this year, these systems were introduced with the Okinawa-based 12th Marine Littoral Regiment, which participated in exercises in the Philippines prior to the Keen Sword drills. With Japan also enhancing its defense capabilities, troops from nine countries—including Australia and France—will join 45,000 Japanese Self-Defense Forces personnel in activities set from October 19 to 29.

The U.S. Army plans to deploy High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) to Camp Ishigaki—roughly 80 miles from Yonaguni—as part of the exercise. Additionally, the Army’s Typhon missile launcher will be transferred to Okinawa mid-month, although its involvement in the exercise has not been publicly confirmed.

In a deviation from past iterations, where naval assets like the USS George Washington participated, this year’s exercise marks a shift toward a land-based network of mobile systems. Last year, the focus was on utilizing Yonaguni as a forward operating base, whereas this year will emphasize Japan’s long-range standoff-strike capabilities, including the new Type-25 surface-to-ship guided missile system.

This shift comes against a backdrop of increasing tension in the Taiwan Strait, with Japanese and U.S. exercises ramping up amid Chinese incursions into Japanese waters. Reports indicate that Chinese coast guard vessels have entered Japan’s exclusive economic zone near Yonaguni, exacerbating concerns over regional security.

Local officials in Yonaguni have expressed apprehension about the implications of large-scale military exercises on the civilian population. They have asked residents to avoid certain roads during the transportation of military equipment through Kubura Port for the exercise. In light of previous incidents involving military aircraft, such as a ground-strike incident involving a Japan Self-Defense Forces V-22 Osprey, local leadership has indicated that the island is not yet prepared for extensive military operations.

Yonaguni Mayor Tsuneo Uechi noted that while the island recognizes the necessity for military training, the scale of the exercises must be manageable to ensure the community’s capacity is not exceeded. The local government continues to engage in discussions with the defense ministry, emphasizing concerns over civilian safety and infrastructure as they prepare for the upcoming exercise.
